The moral influence (or moral exemplar) theory holds that the primary saving effect of Christ's life and death is on human hearts. Humanity's problem is not that God is unwilling to forgive, but that we are estranged, fearful and unloving toward God. In Christ, especially in his willingness to suffer and die for his enemies, God displays a love so great that it awakens answering love in us. This love frees us from the fear of punishment, moves us to repentance, and unites us to God, and by it we are justified and transformed.

Peter Abelard is regarded as its originator because of a famous passage in his commentary on Romans 3, though his own theology also uses language of Christ bearing our sins and interceding for us. The view became prominent in nineteenth- and twentieth-century liberal Protestantism (Schleiermacher in a qualified way, Horace Bushnell, Hastings Rashdall) and remains attractive to those who find objective models morally troubling. Almost all traditions include a moral-influence element; the debate is whether it is the whole of atonement or one effect of a deeper objective work.

Abelard taught in Paris in an age when Anselm had recently rejected the devil's rights. Abelard went further, asking why God would need any price, whether to the devil or to himself: how could the death of an innocent please God? His answer was that God, out of love, became human and persevered in teaching us by word and example unto death, binding us to himself by love. Bernard of Clairvaux denounced this as reducing Christ's work to example, and the Council of Sens (1141) condemned propositions drawn from Abelard's teaching.

The view revived in the Enlightenment and nineteenth century amid moral objections to penal theories (Socinians had already argued that God could forgive freely). Bushnell, Ritschl, Rashdall and others developed it. Twentieth-century critics such as P. T. Forsyth and James Denney argued that love shown by an act that achieves nothing is not intelligible. Contemporary scholars often note that Abelard himself combined this emphasis with other themes, and that subjective effects are affirmed in virtually every tradition alongside objective ones.

Penal substitution holds that on the cross Christ bore, in the place of sinners, the penalty that God's justice rightly requires for sin. God is holy and just; sin is not only a debt of honour but a violation of his law that deserves condemnation, death and wrath. Because God is also loving, he does not abandon sinners to that judgment, but neither does he set justice aside. Instead God himself, in the person of his Son, takes the penalty upon himself. Christ's death propitiates God's wrath and expiates sin, so that God is both 'just and the justifier' of those who have faith in Jesus (Rom 3:26). Through faith, believers are united to Christ: their sin is reckoned to him and his righteousness is reckoned (imputed) to them.

Defenders stress that this is not an angry Father punishing an unwilling third party: the Father, Son and Spirit act together in love; the Son freely gives himself; and the substitution is possible because Christ is both God and the representative head united with his people. John Stott called it the 'self-substitution of God'. Most proponents hold it alongside other models, often arguing that substitution is the foundation that makes victory, example and reconciliation possible.

Elements of penal substitution appear in patristic writers (e.g. Eusebius of Caesarea and others speak of Christ bearing our punishment), though defenders and critics dispute how central such statements are. The view was systematized in the Reformation, when Luther and Calvin recast Anselm's satisfaction in terms of law, penalty and the curse, linking it closely to justification by faith alone and imputed righteousness. Socinians attacked it in the late sixteenth century; Reformed scholastics such as Turretin defended it, and it became standard in Protestant confessions (e.g. the Westminster Confession speaks of Christ fully satisfying the justice of his Father).

In the twentieth century C. H. Dodd argued that hilastērion means expiation rather than propitiation, and Leon Morris answered him. Since the 1990s the view has been sharply criticized (e.g. Joel Green and Mark Baker; Steve Chalke's 2003 'cosmic child abuse' remark), and vigorously defended (Pierced for Our Transgressions, 2007). Most defenders today hold it as the central model among several and affirm Christus Victor and exemplary themes alongside it.

The governmental theory, associated with the Dutch jurist and theologian Hugo Grotius, views God chiefly as the moral Ruler of the universe rather than as a private creditor or offended party. As Ruler, God may lawfully relax the penalty of his law for the sake of mercy, but he cannot simply ignore sin without weakening the authority of his moral government and encouraging further rebellion. Christ's death is therefore a public exhibition of God's hatred of sin and of what sin deserves. It is a genuine penal example, suffered by Christ on behalf of sinners, but it is not the exact equivalent of the punishment each sinner owed.

Because the law's authority has been vindicated before the universe, God can freely pardon those who repent and believe without compromising justice. Grotius presented the view as a defence of the 'catholic' doctrine of satisfaction against Socinus, but it became a distinct model. It was developed in New England theology (Jonathan Edwards Jr., Joseph Bellamy), in Charles Finney's revivalism, and in Methodist systematics (John Miley), where it fitted Arminian convictions that Christ died for all and that salvation is conditional on faith.
